title: XSS Fundamentals
summary: Cross-site scripting is attacker code running inside your origin with your user's full privileges. Learn the stored, reflected and DOM-based varieties, and why the third one never touches your server.

slides.markdown:
**Cross-site scripting (XSS)** is the bug where data you accepted from a user gets treated as *code* by another user's browser. One unescaped comment field, and a stranger's JavaScript is running on your domain, in your victim's logged-in session.

It has been in the OWASP Top 10 since the list existed, and it is still the single most common vulnerability class reported through bug-bounty programs. Frontend engineers own it, because almost every fix lives in the rendering layer.

The thing to internalise first is not the payloads — it's the **boundary**. Every place your app takes a string it did not author and puts it into HTML, an attribute, a URL, or a script context is a boundary, and XSS is what happens when that boundary is crossed without encoding.

This topic covers what XSS is and its three varieties. The fix — context-aware encoding, framework auto-escaping, and sanitizers — is the next topic.

slides.subTitle: Attacker code, your origin
slides.markdown:
The browser's whole security model is the **same-origin policy**: code from `evil.example` cannot read data belonging to `bank.example`. XSS is the bug that makes that irrelevant, because the attacker's script *is* served by `bank.example` as far as the browser can tell.

Mechanically, three things have to line up:

- Your app accepts a string from an untrusted source — a form field, a query parameter, a URL fragment, a header, a value pulled back out of your own database.
- That string reaches a **sink** that interprets markup or code: `innerHTML`, `document.write`, an attribute value, a `<script>` block, an `href`.
- Nothing encoded it on the way, so `<script>` arrives as a tag rather than as five printable characters.

Once that happens the attacker's code inherits the origin. It can read the DOM, call your API with the user's cookies attached, and read anything in `localStorage`. See [same-origin-policy-and-cors](same-origin-policy-and-cors) for the model XSS defeats.

slides.subTitle: Where the payload lives and how it travels
slides.markdown:
The three classic varieties differ in **where the untrusted string rests between the attack and the victim** — which changes who is reachable and who can fix it.

| | Stored | Reflected | DOM-based |
|---|---|---|---|
| Payload lives in | your database / cache | the request URL or form post | never leaves the browser |
| Delivery | victim just visits the page | victim must open a crafted link | victim opens a crafted link or fragment |
| Server sees it? | yes, on write and on read | yes, in the request | **no** — often not even in server logs |
| Blast radius | everyone who views the record | one victim per link | one victim per link |
| Fix belongs to | write path or render path | render path | client JavaScript only |

Stored is the most severe because it needs no social engineering — a poisoned display name renders for every viewer, which is how self-propagating worms like the 2005 Samy worm on MySpace spread to a million profiles in under a day.

DOM-based is the most often missed, because a server-side scan or a WAF sitting in front of the app never observes the payload at all.

slides.sectionTitle: The path of a stored payload
slides.subTitle: Comment field to victim's browser
slides.markdown:
Trace a stored XSS end to end and it becomes obvious why the render path is where the fix belongs.

1. The attacker posts a comment whose body is markup rather than prose. Your API validates it is under 2,000 characters and stores it verbatim.
2. Days later, an unrelated logged-in user opens the thread. Your server or your client fetches the comment and injects the body into the page.
3. The browser parses that body as HTML. There is no marker distinguishing it from the markup your template authored, so the attacker's script executes as first-party code.
4. It now runs with the victim's session. It can call your own API endpoints and the victim's cookies ride along automatically.

Notice the attacker and the victim are never online at the same time, and nothing about step 3 looks unusual in a log. The single moment where the outcome is decided is step 2 — whether the string was encoded for the context it landed in.

slides.subTitle: innerHTML from user input
It runs with the victim's full privileges
slides.markdown:
Junior engineers under-rate XSS because the demo is a popup. The correct mental model: **an XSS is a remote code execution inside your user's session**. Injected script can do anything that user could do by clicking, only silently and instantly.

Concretely, script running in your origin can:

- **Call your own API** with the session cookie attached automatically — change the account email, add an OAuth app, transfer funds. It never needs to read the cookie to use it.
- **Read the DOM**, so anything on screen is exfiltratable: account numbers, a one-time code the user just pasted, the contents of a form mid-typing.
- **Read `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`**, which is exactly where many apps park a JWT.
- **Rewrite the page**, including replacing the login form with a look-alike that posts credentials elsewhere. The URL bar and the TLS padlock stay correct, so every signal a careful user checks still says the site is genuine.
- **Persist**, by registering a service worker or planting itself into stored content so it re-executes.

That last bullet is why XSS on an authenticated page is routinely triaged as critical rather than medium.

slides.subTitle: Sources and sinks, no server involved
slides.markdown:
**DOM-based XSS** happens entirely in client JavaScript: untrusted data flows from a *source* to a *sink* without ever making a round trip you control.

Common **sources** — attacker-influenceable values already in the page:

- `location.search`, `location.hash`, `location.pathname`, `document.referrer`
- `postMessage` event data from another window
- values read back out of `localStorage` or a cookie

Common **sinks** — APIs that parse what you give them:

- `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`
- `eval`, `new Function`, `setTimeout` with a string argument
- assigning to `element.src` / `a.href` where a `javascript:` URL executes

The URL fragment deserves special attention: **everything after `#` is never sent to the server**. A payload in the fragment appears in no access log, is invisible to a WAF, and shows up in no server-side scan — yet reaches any client code that reads `location.hash`. This is why a report of "XSS on our marketing page" can be entirely real even when the backend team can find nothing.

slides.sectionTitle: A DOM XSS the server never sees

slides.markdown:
The reasoning sounds airtight and is wrong. "Stored" means the payload **persists somewhere between the attacker's visit and the victim's**, and a relational database is only the most obvious somewhere.

Stores that have all produced real stored-XSS findings:

- **A CDN or edge cache** holding a rendered page that contained a reflected payload — now every visitor gets it, not just the one who clicked the link.
- **`localStorage` on a shared or kiosk machine**, replayed into the DOM on the next session.
- **A log viewer or admin dashboard** rendering a `User-Agent` or username straight from request logs. The victim here is your own support engineer, who is usually the highest-privileged user you have.
- **Uploaded files served from your origin.** An SVG is XML and can carry a script element; served as `image/svg+xml` from your domain and opened directly, it executes in your origin.
- **A third-party CMS, feature-flag description, or error-tracking payload** rendered unescaped in an internal tool.

The generalisation: ask *where does untrusted text come to rest and later get rendered*, not *do we have a database*.

slides.sectionTitle: Sinks that don't look like sinks
slides.markdown:
Most people learn to distrust `innerHTML` and stop there. The sinks that survive code review are the ones that look like plain data binding.

- **A user-controlled `href`.** `<a href={userUrl}>` looks inert, but `javascript:` is a URL scheme, and clicking it executes. React will warn but historically did not block it. Validate the scheme is `http:` or `https:` before binding.
- **A user-controlled image or iframe `src`**, same reasoning, plus `data:` URLs which can carry HTML.
- **An unquoted attribute in a hand-built template string.** With `<div class=%s>`, a value containing a space introduces a whole new attribute — an event handler, for instance — without ever needing an angle bracket. Quoting the attribute closes that path.
- **`setTimeout('doThing(' + id + ')', 100)`** — the string form of `setTimeout` is `eval` wearing a hat.
- **Markdown rendering with raw HTML enabled.** Many renderers pass through inline HTML by default; that is a documented feature and an open sink.
- **Server-rendered JSON dropped inside a `<script>` block.** The sequence that closes a script tag inside a JSON string ends the block early, whatever your JSON encoder thought.

Each of these is safe with the right encoding for *its* context — which is the whole subject of the next topic, Preventing XSS.

slides.sectionTitle: What HttpOnly does and doesn't buy
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A common half-truth: "we set `HttpOnly` on the session cookie, so XSS can't hurt us."

`HttpOnly` is genuinely valuable — it stops `document.cookie` from reading the session token, which closes the **exfiltration** path. An attacker cannot lift the cookie and replay it from their own machine tomorrow.

What it does not close is the **use** path. The browser attaches that cookie to same-origin requests automatically, so injected script can simply call your API from the victim's page and act as them, right now:

- `POST /api/account/email` to take over the account
- `POST /api/tokens` to mint a long-lived API key the attacker *can* read
- read any endpoint's response and ship the data out, which is the same outcome as stealing the cookie, one step later

So the accurate framing is: `HttpOnly` downgrades XSS from "permanent account takeover from anywhere" to "complete control of the session while the page is open, plus whatever persistence the attacker can bootstrap." That is a real reduction and nowhere near a fix. Storage trade-offs get their own topic later in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: How XSS is found and rated
slides.markdown:
Useful context for the day a report lands in your queue.

**How it gets found.** Researchers spray a canary string through every input and search the rendered DOM for it, then check whether it landed inside a tag, an attribute, a URL, or a script block — the context determines whether it is exploitable. Automated DAST scanners do the same thing at scale; DOM-based cases need a headless browser, which is why server-side scanners miss them.

**How it gets rated.** Severity is driven by three questions, not by cleverness of the payload: does it need authentication, does it need the victim to click something, and does it persist? Stored XSS on an authenticated page with no interaction is typically triaged critical; reflected XSS behind a crafted link on an anonymous marketing page is often medium.

**What actually removes the class.** Individually patching sinks is whack-a-mole. The durable answers are structural: a framework that escapes by default, a sanitizer at the one place raw HTML is genuinely needed, and a strict Content Security Policy as the layer that limits what an injection can *do* even when one slips through. The rest of this group builds each of those.
